prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I opened with IceCube first and optical lattice clocks second, and after reading the eight ballots I move optical lattice clocks to the top of my preferred configuration. The case is that it combines a simple, original idea (Katori's magic-wavelength trapping) with a decisive experimental realisation (Ye's strontium clock at the 1e-18 level), and it has been independently reproduced and intercompared across continents with Sr, Yb and Hg for about twenty years. It enables tests of relativistic redshift over millimetres, searches for varying constants and dark matter, and a probable redefinition of the second. It is a measurement-driven advance of the kind I value as an instrument builder. Seven of eight members ranked it, three put it first and four put it in their top three, and the credited pair is the cleanest attribution on the shortlist. A one-achievement, two-laureate prize is compact and defensible, and I would rather build consensus on the candidate with the least dispute over who did what than on one I personally favour.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that precision atomic timekeeping has been rewarded repeatedly (Ramsey 1989, Hall and Hansch 2005, Wineland and Haroche 2012), so the committee could see optical lattice clocks as an incremental step in a line already honoured, and the second has not yet been redefined. Lindroth and Kroll both name this overlap risk. Ye's name also spans combs, clocks and molecules, so the citation must be drawn tightly. I also have to admit that this is outside my own expertise: I can judge calibration, systematics and reproducibility, but I cannot adjudicate priority between Katori and the Ye group, or the roles of Lemonde, Takamoto and others, and I would want expert reviewers on the early history. Finally, a clock result is less of a discovery from nature than a window on the universe, which is where my own taste leans toward IceCube.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first because the magic-wavelength idea is simple and decisive, Katori and Ye are a clean pair, and the redefinition of the second makes timing right; he accepts the risk of overlap with the comb prize.
responses.response: I agree on the science and the attribution, and I now put it first. I would qualify the timing argument: the pending redefinition of the second is a reason the community will celebrate, but the prize case should not depend on a decision of a metrology body. It stands on the reproducibility of 1e-18 clocks alone. I would also push back a little on your ranking of IceCube eighth: your objection is attribution inside a large collaboration, and I accept that, but it is an argument about whom to name, not about the physics, which is firmly established.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks optical lattice clocks first as a natural successor to the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes, but flags that the committee may see it as a continuation of a line already honoured, and that Ye's scope is broad.
responses.response: This is the serious objection and I take it seriously. My answer is that the lattice clock is a distinct invention, not a refinement of the comb or of ion trapping: trapping many atoms with the light shift cancelled changes the statistics and the systematics, which is why it overtook ion clocks. I would therefore keep the citation narrow to the lattice-clock concept and its realisation, and I would not credit Ye for combs or molecules. If you or Kroll feel the overlap is too heavy, I would like to hear which part of the claim you think is already covered by 2005 or 2012.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube first as a new window on the universe built on an instrument in Antarctic ice, with independent analyses and the Galactic-plane result supporting the diffuse flux, while noting that credit is difficult in a large collaboration.
responses.response: We agree on the physics, and it was my own first choice. My difficulty is the attribution, which you also note: Halzen and Karle are the natural pair, yet Yoshida, the AMANDA history and the multi-messenger source work make any two or three names open to challenge, and individual sources are still at a few sigma. I keep IceCube as my first alternative and would support it in a later round if we can obtain a reliable historical review of the roles. It cannot be combined with optical lattice clocks in the same year without exceeding three people, so we need to decide which one carries the year.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first as a prediction-then-confirmation story with a Bistritzer-MacDonald theory credit and a Jarillo-Herrero experimental credit, and ranks optical lattice clocks last of the eight, partly deferring to atomic physics colleagues.
responses.response: I take the point that moire physics has transformed condensed matter, and I keep it as my second alternative. I have two qualifications. The experimental first author, Yuan Cao, is not in the credited names, which is a fairness problem you also mention, and the pairing mechanism remains unsettled, so the interpretation is not yet stable. I do not equate your lower ranking of clocks with weaker science, since you say it is outside your field; I would ask whether anything in the clock case is a substantive objection beyond expertise, because the maturity of the clock work is the strongest of any candidate on the list.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as a controllable single-photon, single-artificial-atom platform that underlies transmon processors, noting his closeness to the field and the sensitivity of the 2025 prize in superconducting circuits.
responses.response: I accept that circuit QED is mature and very influential, and I ranked it fifth for that reason. My reservation is the timing: the 2025 prize to Clarke, Devoret and Martinis is for the same hardware family, and a four-name candidate with a theory-versus-experiment split forces an uncomfortable choice of three. You flag your own possible bias and I appreciate that; I would be interested in whether you think the circuit QED case is strong enough to stand a year after the 2025 prize or whether it is better in two or three years.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards optical lattice clocks as distinct from the frequency-comb (2005) and ion-trapping (2012) prizes.
Priority and credit between Katori and Ye's group, and the roles of other early lattice-clock groups, which I cannot judge as an astroparticle experimentalist.
Whether a two-person, single-achievement prize is preferable to a combined configuration, given that the IceCube names and the clock names together would exceed three people.
The IceCube credit allocation (Halzen, Karle, Yoshida, AMANDA history) is unresolved and needs expert historical advice.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the preferred candidate. I note that I am an astroparticle experimentalist in the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations, which may bias me toward IceCube and which I disclose; I have no apparent connection to the IceCube collaboration or to the lattice-clock groups. As Chair I will run the process neutrally.
